claims.text: The proposed intervention is to deposit an approximately 1–2 nm graphene layer on tungsten particles by CVD, apply an adhesion-promoting treatment, and then infiltrate the particles with copper.
The intervention will produce a nanoscale graphene interphase at the tungsten–copper boundary.
The adhesion promoter will create strong bonding at the graphene-containing tungsten–copper interface.
Graphene has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
The graphene interphase will act as a thermal bridge across the tungsten–copper interface.
The graphene interphase will lower the Kapitza resistance of the tungsten–copper interface.
Lower interfacial thermal resistance will increase the effective thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The adhesion-promoting treatment will keep the interface mechanically robust during thermal cycling.
The adhesion-promoting treatment will safeguard the composite against irradiation-related degradation.
The modified composite will have approximately 10–20% or greater effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable conventional W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will retain mechanical properties comparable to those of a conventional W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will have enhanced resistance to irradiation-induced damage relative to a conventional W–Cu composite.
The predicted benefits are expected to hold under fusion-joint conditions involving temperatures up to approximately 500°C, high heat flux, and neutron irradiation.
Applicability at temperatures or irradiation levels significantly beyond the stated fusion-joint conditions is uncertain.
The exact conductivity improvement and long-term mechanical and irradiation behavior require experimental validation.
The ability of the adhesion promoter to preserve interface integrity under cyclic thermal and irradiation stresses is not established.
